name: Superior colliculus
function: Multimodal orienting center of the tectum: builds a retinotopic and spatiotopic map on which salient visual (and auditory/somatosensory) stimuli trigger saccades and combined eye-head turning; its rostral pretectal neighbours relay the pupillary light reflex, while the colliculus itself drives orienting saccades and eye-head turning. Its output gates orienting movement via tectospinal and tectobulbar projections.

afferent: Retina (direct retinotectal fibers and via the optic tract)
Striate and extrastriate visual cortex (corticotectal fibers)
Substantia nigra, pars reticulata (tonic GABAergic gating)
efferent: Tectospinal tract (crosses in the dorsal tegmental decussation to contralateral neck/upper cord)
Tectobulbar fibers to the PPRF and CN III/IV/VI nuclei for saccade initiation
Pulvinar and pretectal area
Brainstem reticular formation

bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the posterior cerebral artery; lateral portion also receives branches of the superior cerebellar artery

clinical.findings: Dorsal midbrain compression or infarction involving the superior colliculus/pretectal region impairs vertical saccades and the pupillary light reflex (light-near dissociation).
clinical.vascular: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA; pineal region mass effect

clinical.findings: Experimental collicular lesions impair initiation of reflexive saccades toward peripheral targets and visual attention shifting, while voluntary scanning is relatively preserved (cortical saccade generation is intact).
clinical.note: Rarely isolated in humans; derived mainly from lesion and stimulation studies.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 11, geniculate/extrageniculate pathways, printed pp. 464-465 (PDF pp. 490-491).

name: Inferior colliculus
function: Obligatory integrative relay of the central auditory pathway: nearly all ascending auditory fibers converge here in a tonotopic map that preserves binaural timing- and intensity-based sound localization cues, before output continues through the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus. Also participates in auditory startle and orienting responses.

afferent: Lateral lemniscus (from cochlear nuclei and superior olivary complex)
Contralateral inferior colliculus (commissure of the inferior colliculus)
efferent: Brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN)
Commissural fibers to the contralateral inferior colliculus
Superior colliculus and reticular formation (auditory orienting/startle)

bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the posterior cerebral artery; caudal branches of the superior cerebellar artery

clinical.findings: Small lesions of the inferior colliculus degrade sound localization and hearing quality without causing unilateral deafness, because auditory pathways are bilaterally represented at and above this level.
clinical.vascular: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA or SCA

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 11, geniculate/extrageniculate pathways, printed pp. 464-465 (PDF pp. 490-491).

Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, vertical gaze, printed pp. 587-588 (PDF pp. 613-614).

name: Pretectal area
function: Pretectal region rostral to the superior colliculi. The olivary pretectal light-reflex relay receives retinal input and projects bilaterally to preganglionic parasympathetic oculomotor neurons, partly through the posterior commissure. Nearby rostral-midbrain gaze circuitry is distinct from this pupillary relay.

afferent: Retina via the optic tract (brachium of the superior colliculus region)
efferent: Bilateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei (partly crossing through the posterior commissure)
Superior colliculus
Medial rectus subnuclei (near-triad coordination)

bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the posterior cerebral artery

clinical.syndrome: Light-near dissociation in dorsal midbrain disease
clinical.findings: Pretectal/posterior-commissural injury can impair the pupillary light response while sparing the near response, often with other dorsal-midbrain findings. The historical Argyll Robertson pupil is a clinical association with neurosyphilis, not a precisely established isolated pretectal lesion locator.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 11, geniculate/extrageniculate pathways, printed pp. 464-465 (PDF pp. 490-491).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, pupillary circuits, printed pp. 576-580 (PDF pp. 602-606).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, vertical gaze, printed pp. 587-588 (PDF pp. 613-614).

name: Periaqueductal gray
function: Central hub of endogenous pain modulation: the PAG is densely packed with mu-opioid receptors, and stimulation releases endogenous opioids that activate a descending analgesia pathway (PAG to rostral ventromedial medulla and locus coeruleus-side noradrenergic systems to the dorsal horn). It also organizes autonomic and behavioral responses to threat and stress, including fight-or-flight cardiovascular changes, defensive behavior, micturition, and vocalization.

efferent: Nucleus raphe magnus and medullary reticular formation (descending analgesia)
Locus coeruleus (noradrenergic pain modulation)
Hypothalamus and brainstem autonomic nuclei (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor vagal nucleus)
Cuneiform/pedunculopontine region (defensive locomotion)

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip and proximal posterior cerebral artery (posterior thalamoperforating territory); collicular branches dorsally

clinical.findings: PAG circuitry participates in descending pain modulation and defensive/autonomic responses. Effects of focal injury are variable; PAG stimulation has been studied for refractory pain but should not be presented as a broadly established routine therapy.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, pain modulation, printed pp. 282-283 (PDF pp. 308-309).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, reticular/autonomic systems, printed pp. 646-648 (PDF pp. 672-674).

name: Oculomotor nucleus (CN III)
function: Somatic motor nuclear complex in the rostral midbrain at the superior-collicular level. Medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique subnuclei mainly supply ipsilateral muscles; the superior-rectus subnucleus supplies the contralateral muscle, and a midline central caudal subnucleus supplies both levators. Nuclear injury may therefore produce bilateral ptosis or superior-rectus deficits rather than a simple unilateral nerve pattern.

afferent: Medial longitudinal fasciculus from contralateral abducens internuclear neurons (conjugate horizontal gaze)
Rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal (vertical gaze holding)
efferent: CN III fascicles running ventrally through the red nucleus to exit in the interpeduncular fossa
Extraocular muscles (medial/superior/inferior rectus, inferior oblique) and levator palpebrae

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery (posterior thalamoperforating); the exiting nerve passes between PCA and SCA

clinical.findings: Nuclear injury can cause bilateral or asymmetric ocular motor deficits. Fascicular injury may give ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral weakness or ataxia according to neighboring pathways.
A new CN III palsy can reflect compressive, ischemic or other disease. Pupil involvement raises concern for aneurysmal compression, but pupil sparing does not exclude a dangerous compressive cause.

name: Edinger-Westphal preganglionic neurons
function: Preganglionic parasympathetic neurons associated with the oculomotor complex whose axons travel in CN III to the ciliary ganglion. Postganglionic neurons then supply sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. These EWpg neurons must be distinguished from centrally projecting Edinger-Westphal (EWcp) neurons, which have different functions and are not the pupillary motor relay.

afferent: Bilateral pretectal inputs for the light reflex
efferent: Preganglionic parasympathetic axons in CN III to the ciliary ganglion; postganglionic short ciliary nerves supply the pupil sphincter and ciliary muscle

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: EWpg or outgoing parasympathetic-fiber injury can impair pupil constriction and accommodation. Light-near dissociation reflects differential pathway disruption; a peripheral autonomic lesion does not automatically establish pretectal-to-EW interruption.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, ocular motor nuclei and pupils, printed pp. 568-580 (PDF pp. 594-606).

name: Trochlear nucleus (CN IV)
function: Innervates the contralateral superior oblique muscle via CN IV, which depresses, intorts, and abducts the globe. CN IV is unique: its fibers curve dorsally around the cerebral aqueduct, decussate completely in the superior medullary velum, and exit the dorsal midbrain just below the inferior colliculus — the only cranial nerve with a fully crossed intramedullary course and a dorsal exit.

afferent: Medial longitudinal fasciculus (vestibulo-ocular and internuclear input)
Rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF (vertical saccade generation)
Cuneiform nucleus and mesencephalic reticular formation
efferent: CN IV fibers around the aqueduct decussating in the superior medullary velum
Contralateral superior oblique muscle

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: A trochlear nuclear or pre-crossing fascicular lesion affects the contralateral superior oblique; a post-crossing nerve lesion affects the ipsilateral muscle. Superior-oblique weakness causes vertical/torsional diplopia, often worse in downgaze and contralateral gaze relative to the weak eye, with hypertropia increased by head tilt toward that eye.
Dorsal crossing or nerve injury may affect both superior obliques after trauma. Bilateral findings are variable and do not prove the precise exit-zone site.

name: Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus
function: A column of pseudounipolar primary sensory neurons embedded within the CNS — the only such group in the brain: these cells are the proprioceptive ganglion for the masticatory muscles and periodontal ligament, conveying jaw position and bite-force information and serving as the afferent limb of the monosynaptic jaw-jerk reflex. Extends from the rostral pons through the midbrain.

afferent: Peripheral processes of mesencephalic trigeminal primary sensory neurons carry jaw-muscle-spindle and periodontal input through CN V; their cell bodies lie in the CNS rather than the trigeminal ganglion.
efferent: Monosynaptic collateral to the trigeminal motor nucleus (jaw-jerk reflex arc)
Cerebellar connections via the superior cerebellar peduncle region

bloodSupply: Branches of the superior cerebellar artery (dorsolateral tegmentum); paramedian perforators medially

clinical.findings: The mesencephalic trigeminal system supplies proprioceptive input to jaw motor reflexes. Damage may reduce this arc; an exaggerated jaw jerk usually indicates bilateral supranuclear corticobulbar disease, not damage to this sensory nucleus.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, mesencephalic trigeminal system, printed pp. 510-512 (PDF pp. 536-538).

name: Mesencephalic trigeminal tract
function: Slender fiber bundle running along the lateral edge of the periaqueductal gray through the dorsolateral midbrain and rostral pons, carrying the central processes and reflex collaterals of the mesencephalic trigeminal neurons — the afferent limb of the jaw-jerk reflex.

afferent: Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus neuron processes (jaw proprioception)
efferent: Trigeminal motor nucleus (monosynaptic jaw-jerk arc)
Cerebellum (proprioceptive information)

bloodSupply: Superior cerebellar artery branches (dorsolateral tegmentum)

clinical.findings: Injury may disturb jaw proprioceptive information or the jaw-jerk reflex. Isolated human tract syndromes are uncommon, so neither a guaranteed deficit nor complete asymptomaticity can be inferred from this schematic.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, mesencephalic trigeminal system, printed pp. 510-512 (PDF pp. 536-538).

name: Red nucleus
function: Motor-related nucleus of the rostral midbrain tegmentum. Its caudal magnocellular division gives rise to the crossed rubrospinal pathway, much less developed in humans than in many other mammals. Its rostral parvocellular division receives cerebellar and cortical inputs and projects to the ipsilateral inferior olive through the central tegmental tract. Cerebellothalamic fibers also pass through or around the red-nucleus region en route to the thalamus; these differ from fibers terminating in the red nucleus.

afferent: Contralateral deep cerebellar nuclei through the crossed superior cerebellar peduncle
efferent: Magnocellular rubrospinal fibers cross in the ventral tegmental decussation
Parvocellular rubro-olivary fibers descend toward the ipsilateral inferior olive through the central tegmental tract
Cerebellothalamic axons pass through/around the red-nuclear region toward thalamus; this is not a red-nucleus-to-contralateral-thalamus relay

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the basilar tip / PCA (medial red nucleus); branches of the superior cerebellar artery (lateral)

clinical.findings: CN III fascicular injury with neighboring cerebellothalamic pathway injury can combine ipsilateral ophthalmoparesis with contralateral ataxia or tremor (Claude/Benedikt patterns). Historical eponym boundaries vary.
Delayed low-frequency rest, postural and action tremor can follow lesions of distributed cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal networks. It should not be localized exclusively to the red nucleus.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar output/input pathways, printed pp. 705-710 (PDF pp. 731-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), midbrain sections and SCP crossing, printed pp. 136-144 (PDF pp. 150-158).

name: Substantia nigra, pars compacta
function: Neuromelanin-containing dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta. Nigrostriatal projections to caudate and putamen modulate direct and indirect basal-ganglia pathways. Mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine projections arise mainly from the neighboring ventral tegmental area, rather than being defining SNc outputs.

afferent: Subthalamic and brainstem inputs, including pedunculopontine and raphe systems
efferent: Nigrostriatal dopaminergic projections to caudate and putamen

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the posterior cerebral artery; anterior choroidal artery branches (lateral/caudal portions)

clinical.findings: Degeneration of SNc dopaminergic neurons contributes to bradykinesia, rigidity and often rest tremor. Nonmotor symptoms may precede motor diagnosis; postural instability is often later. A fixed cell-loss threshold or mandatory symptom tetrad should not be used as a diagnostic rule.
Rare focal nigral lesions can produce parkinsonism. More typical vascular parkinsonism involves broader subcortical vascular disease, and the phenotype depends on affected networks.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, basal-ganglia circuits, printed pp. 748-754 (PDF pp. 774-780).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, Parkinson disease and related disorders, printed pp. 762-768 (PDF pp. 788-794).
NINDS, Parkinson Disease, https://www.ninds.nih.gov/current-research/focus-disorders/parkinsons-disease-research/parkinsons-disease-challenges-progress-and-promise.

name: Substantia nigra, pars reticulata
function: One of the two GABAergic output nuclei of the basal ganglia (with the internal globus pallidus): SNr neurons fire tonically and tonically inhibit the superior colliculus and thalamus. Corticostriatal excitation of the direct pathway inhibits the SNr, disinhibiting collicular saccade circuits and thalamocortical motor loops; the indirect pathway (via the subthalamic nucleus) increases SNr output and suppresses movement.

efferent: Superior colliculus (reflexive saccade gating)
VA/VL and mediodorsal thalamus
Pedunculopontine nucleus

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the PCA; anterior choroidal artery branches laterally

clinical.findings: SNr is a tonic inhibitory basal-ganglia output nucleus with thalamic, collicular and brainstem targets. Injury or network dysfunction can disturb movement and eye-movement control, but an isolated human lesion does not define a predictable hyperkinetic or visually distractible syndrome.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, basal-ganglia circuits, printed pp. 748-754 (PDF pp. 774-780).

name: Crus cerebri
function: Ventral midbrain descending fiber compartment (basis pedunculi). Medial fibers are predominantly frontopontine, the middle part carries corticospinal/corticobulbar fibers, and lateral fibers include temporoparieto-occipitopontine projections. This is a broad topographic scheme, not a strictly separated fiber map. Corticospinal fibers continue through the pons to the medullary pyramids.

afferent: Internal capsule (genu and posterior limb): corticobulbar, corticospinal, and corticopontine fibers
efferent: Basis pontis (corticopontine fibers synapse in pontine nuclei)
Medullary pyramids (corticospinal continuation toward the pyramidal decussation)

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries; anterior choroidal artery (lateral crus)

clinical.findings: A medial cerebral-peduncle lesion involving CN III fascicles can cause ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral motor weakness (Weber pattern); completeness, pupil involvement, and weakness distribution or severity depend on lesion extent.
Any crus lesion paired with an ipsilateral third-nerve finding localizes the lesion to the ventral midbrain — the prototype of brainstem crossed syndromes (ipsilateral CN, contralateral body).

name: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussation
synonyms: decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles
function: Crossing of the major dentate/interposed cerebellar efferents in the caudal midbrain near the inferior-collicular level. Crossed fibers reach contralateral red-nuclear and thalamic targets; after the additional crossing in descending motor pathways, each cerebellar hemisphere has a net influence on the ipsilateral body.

afferent: Both superior cerebellar peduncles (dentate and interposed nucleus outflow)
efferent: Contralateral red nucleus
Contralateral VL/VA thalamus
Oculomotor-trochlear nuclear region (collaterals)

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: A lesion centered on the SCP crossing can interrupt output from both cerebellar hemispheres and cause bilateral ataxia. Deficits above or below the crossing depend on which fibers are affected; nearby trochlear/MLF involvement may add ocular motor findings.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar output/input pathways, printed pp. 705-710 (PDF pp. 731-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), midbrain sections and SCP crossing, printed pp. 136-144 (PDF pp. 150-158).

name: Superior cerebellar peduncle
function: Major cerebellar output route from dentate and interposed nuclei through the rostral pons to the caudal-midbrain decussation, then toward contralateral thalamus and red nucleus. It also carries anterior spinocerebellar afferents. Pre-crossing output injury causes mainly ipsilateral limb ataxia; post-crossing cerebellothalamic injury causes contralateral ataxia.

efferent: After decussation: contralateral VL and related motor thalamic targets
After decussation: contralateral red nucleus

bloodSupply: Superior cerebellar artery (pontine portion); paramedian perforators of the basilar tip (midbrain portion)

clinical.findings: The side of ataxia depends on crossing: ipsilateral below the caudal-midbrain SCP decussation, contralateral above it, and potentially bilateral at the crossing.
Delayed Holmes-type tremor can follow cerebellothalamic network injury, often with additional nigrostriatal dysfunction. Side, latency and treatment response vary.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar output/input pathways, printed pp. 705-710 (PDF pp. 731-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), midbrain sections and SCP crossing, printed pp. 136-144 (PDF pp. 150-158).

name: Dorsal raphe nucleus
function: Predominantly serotonergic cell group in the midline periaqueductal region of the midbrain and rostral pons, with major ascending projections to forebrain structures. It modulates arousal, affect and other behaviors. Caudal medullary raphe groups provide important descending spinal serotonergic pain modulation; they should not be conflated with the dorsal raphe.

efferent: Diffuse serotonergic projections to cortex, striatum, thalamus, and hypothalamus
Nucleus raphe magnus (descending pain control)
Interpeduncular nucleus

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: Dorsal raphe neurons participate in distributed serotonergic circuits influencing sleep and affect. SSRIs act on serotonin transporters throughout serotonergic projections, not exclusively on this nucleus; a focal dorsal-raphe lesion is not a specific diagnostic mood syndrome.

name: Cuneiform nucleus
function: Dorsolateral mesencephalic reticular nucleus included with neighboring pedunculopontine circuitry in descriptions of the mesencephalic locomotor region. Experimental and translational studies link this region to locomotion and arousal; precise selective human nuclear lesion functions are not established by this atlas.

efferent: Pontomedullary reticular formation (reticulospinal systems)
Intralaminar thalamus (ascending arousal)
Spinal cord (locomotor and postural control)

bloodSupply: Branches of the superior cerebellar artery and collicular branches of the posterior cerebral artery (dorsolateral tegmentum)

clinical.findings: Mesencephalic locomotor circuitry is studied in gait initiation/freezing and neuromodulation. Freezing of gait has distributed mechanisms and does not uniquely diagnose cuneiform nuclear degeneration.

name: Interpeduncular fossa
function: Ventral midline recess between the two cerebral peduncles, roofed by the posterior perforated substance: CN III rootlets emerge into it, the basilar apex and posterior thalamoperforating vessels course around it, and the interpeduncular cistern fills it with CSF.
bloodSupply: Basilar apex (P1 segments and posterior thalamoperforators); posterior communicating artery branches

clinical.findings: Basilar-apex aneurysm or other cisternal/midbrain disease may affect CN III or nearby pathways. Pupil dysfunction and altered consciousness depend on involvement; top-of-basilar ischemia is distinct from compression by an unruptured aneurysm.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, midbrain sections, printed pp. 615-617 (PDF pp. 641-643).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), midbrain sections, printed pp. 136-144 (PDF pp. 150-158).

name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) exit
synonyms: CN III rootlets in interpeduncular fossa
function: CN III rootlets emerge from the sulcus of the oculomotor nerve on the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle into the interpeduncular fossa, then pass forward between the posterior cerebral artery (above) and the superior cerebellar artery (below) — the vascular interval where aneurysms compress the nerve and paramedian perforators infarct the fascicles (Weber territory).
bloodSupply: PCA/SCA interval perforators; recurrent branches of the posterior communicating artery to the nerve

clinical.findings: CN III palsy may involve ptosis, extraocular weakness and variable pupil dysfunction. Midbrain fascicular extension can add contralateral weakness/ataxia. Acute aneurysmal or herniation-related compression is possible; pupil sparing does not exclude compression.

name: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) exit
synonyms: CN IV dorsal exit below inferior colliculus
function: Dorsal exit of CN IV: the trochlear fibers decussate completely within the superior (anterior) medullary velum and emerge from the dorsal midbrain just caudal to the inferior colliculi — the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem — then wrap around the cerebral peduncle for the longest intracranial subarachnoid course of any cranial nerve, entering the dura at the tentorial edge.
bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the PCA; distal superior cerebellar artery branches

clinical.findings: Trochlear palsy can follow head trauma and may be unilateral or bilateral. Bilateral palsy does not uniquely prove an exit/decussation lesion because peripheral courses can also be injured.

name: Mesencephalon (context surface)
function: Renderable silhouette of the whole mesencephalon as one block: the dorsal tectal plate with its superior and inferior colliculi, the surrounding tegmentum with the cerebral aqueduct, periaqueductal gray, red nuclei and substantia nigra, and the ventral crus cerebri with the interpeduncular fossa between the peduncles. It exists so the midbrain is a single named, selectable body in the 3D scene, not because it is a nucleus; its internal content belongs to the collicular, tegmental and peduncular records.
contextNote: Envelope/context-surface record: the GLB silhouette ctx-midbrain-surface in src/assets/anatomy/anatomy-manifest.json is its 3D body (SceneLayers envelope slot env-midbrain), and its canonical-space extent below is that baked bbox. Not a nucleus — see the collicular, tegmental, peduncular and cranial-nerve records; no plate carries this tag.

afferent: See the individual midbrain records — the envelope itself carries no fibers

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, midbrain sections, printed pp. 615-617 (PDF pp. 641-643).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), midbrain sections, printed pp. 136-144 (PDF pp. 150-158).
